verses.text: Then Jacob went on his journey, and came to the land of the children of the east.
He looked, and behold, a well in the field, and, behold, three flocks of sheep lying there by it. For out of that well they watered the flocks. The stone on the well’s mouth was large.
There all the flocks were gathered. They rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the sheep, and put the stone again on the well’s mouth in its place.
Jacob said to them, “My relatives, where are you from?” They said, “We are from Haran.”
He said to them, “Do you know Laban, the son of Nahor?” They said, “We know him.”
He said to them, “Is it well with him?” They said, “It is well. See, Rachel, his daughter, is coming with the sheep.”
He said, “Behold, it is still the middle of the day, not time to gather the livestock together. Water the sheep, and go and feed them.”
They said, “We can’t, until all the flocks are gathered together, and they roll the stone from the well’s mouth. Then we water the sheep.”
While he was yet speaking with them, Rachel came with her father’s sheep, for she kept them.

When Jacob saw Rachel the daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, and the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother, Jacob went near, and rolled the stone from the well’s mouth, and watered the flock of Laban his mother’s brother.
Jacob kissed Rachel, and lifted up his voice, and wept.
Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s brother, and that he was Rebekah’s son. She ran and told her father.
When Laban heard the news of Jacob, his sister’s son, he ran to meet Jacob, and embraced him, and kissed him, and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban all these things.
Laban said to him, “Surely you are my bone and my flesh.” He lived with him for a month.
Laban said to Jacob, “Because you are my brother, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what will your wages be?”
Laban had two daughters. The name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.
Leah’s eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and attractive.
Jacob loved Rachel. He said, “I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter.”
Laban said, “It is better that I give her to you, than that I should give her to another man. Stay with me.”
Jacob served seven years for Rachel. They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her.
Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her.”
Laban gathered together all the men of the place, and made a feast.
In the evening, he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to him. He went in to her.
Laban gave Zilpah his servant to his daughter Leah for a servant.
In the morning, behold, it was Leah. He said to Laban, “What is this you have done to me? Didn’t I serve with you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?”
Laban said, “It is not done so in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn.
Fulfill the week of this one, and we will give you the other also for the service which you will serve with me yet seven other years.”
Jacob did so, and fulfilled her week. He gave him Rachel his daughter as wife.
Laban gave to Rachel his daughter Bilhah, his servant, to be her servant.
He went in also to Rachel, and he loved also Rachel more than Leah, and served with him yet seven other years.
Yahweh saw that Leah was hated, and he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.
Leah conceived, and bore a son, and she named him Reuben. For she said, “Because Yahweh has looked at my affliction. For now my husband will love me.”
She conceived again, and bore a son, and said, “Because Yahweh has heard that I am hated, he has therefore given me this son also.” She named him Simeon.
She conceived again, and bore a son. Said, “Now this time will my husband be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore his name was called Levi.
She conceived again, and bore a son. She said, “This time will I praise Yahweh.” Therefore she named him Judah. Then she stopped bearing.

footnotes.content: After fleeing from Esau, Jacob turns his feet toward Haran, the land of his people. I have learned that even when we run from trouble, the Lord is gently directing our steps to the place where His purpose will yet meet us. He is faithful to guide us, even when our path looks uncertain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A well in the field, a large stone, and waiting flocks - such ordinary things. I notice how the Lord often meets us at the most unremarkable places. Before Jacob knows it, His providence is already set in motion for the day ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The shepherds must wait together until all the flocks are gathered before rolling the stone away. It reminds me that God's timing often has us wait on one another. There is grace in learning patience, for the Lord's appointments are never rushed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob speaks kindly to strangers, calling them 'my relatives'. A man far from home still seeks his own people. I am grateful that our true family is found not only by blood, but most of all in those who belong to the Lord Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob inquires after Laban, the son of Nahor - his mother's family. The Lord is knitting together the threads He began long ago in Abraham's house. I take comfort that He remembers His promises across generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The shepherds speak well of Laban, and then point to Rachel coming with the sheep. How sweet that the first glimpse of Rachel comes while she is doing her faithful duty. Often the Lord brings His kindness to us in the ordinary work of the day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob, a stranger here, urges the shepherds to water the sheep and go feed them, for there is yet time. I see a man who cares for the sheep of another. It points me to our Good Shepherd, Jesus, who cares for His own even when they belong to others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The custom binds them - they cannot roll the stone until all flocks are gathered. I have learned that sometimes godly order means waiting our turn. The Lord teaches us not to trample others, but to wait for His appointed moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: While Jacob speaks, Rachel draws near with her father's sheep. The Lord times every meeting. I have found that when He is about to show mercy, the very person we need often comes just as we are speaking of the need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seeing Rachel, Jacob rolls the large stone away alone to water Laban's flock. Love stirs him to strength. Yet how much greater is the love of Christ, who for us rolled away a stone far heavier - our sin - and opened the well of living water for all who come to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob kisses Rachel and lifts up his voice and weeps. Such tender emotion from a man of purpose. I think our hearts are not made too soft to weep at kindness after loneliness. The Lord knows the tears of those who have been far from home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob reveals he is Rebekah's son and her father's brother. Rachel runs to tell her father. News travels quickly when the Lord is doing something. I have learned to watch for joy spreading to others when God is merciful to us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban runs to meet him, embraces and kisses him, and brings him home. Kindness flows at first. But I am old enough to know that affection can change when self-interest is touched. We must learn to trust not in man's kindness alone, but in the faithful love of the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Surely you are my bone and my flesh.' Laban speaks warmly, and Jacob stays a month. How quickly we say we are family when it costs us little. The Lord calls us to love our own, but also to be wise, for not all who say 'family' will deal righteously.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban, seeing Jacob's strength, asks for wages. The man who ran to embrace him now counts the cost. I have learned this truth: the world may welcome us for a while, but sooner or later it will ask what we are worth to it. Our true worth is that we are bought by the blood of Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two daughters, Leah the elder, Rachel the younger. Scripture names them simply. I note the Lord is about to show us that He looks past outward order and chooses in ways that confound our expectations. His grace often rests where men would not look.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and attractive. The world measures by beauty, but the Lord measures the heart. I have lived long enough to see how fleeting outward beauty is, and how precious it is to be lovely to the One who loves us for Jesus' sake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob loves Rachel and offers seven years of service for her. Such love is strong, yet earthly love is also capable of blindness. How blessed we are that the love of Jesus is not blind to our sin, but chose us anyway and paid the full price for us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban says it is better to give her to Jacob than to another. He speaks of propriety, but his heart is already scheming. I have learned to be grateful for those who deal truly, and to pray that the Lord would guard us from those who use fair words for crooked ends.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob serves seven years for Rachel; they seem but a few days for the love he had for her. What a picture of love that endures toil for the one it loves. I think of our Lord, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross to win His bride, the Church (Hebrews 12:2). That love alone will never fail.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The days are fulfilled, and Jacob asks for his wife. After long hope, the heart longs for what was promised. How much more ought our hearts to long for our promised Bridegroom, Jesus, when every earthly hope has run its course.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban gathers all the men of the place and makes a feast. Feasting can be innocent, but here it covers deceit. I have learned to be wary when revelry hides a trap. Our Lord calls us to speak the truth, and to rejoice in truth alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the evening, Laban brings Leah to Jacob, and he goes in to her. Jacob, who deceived his father by night (Genesis 27), is now deceived in the darkness by his uncle. The Lord is not mocked; He deals justly, yet He also uses even such sorrow to accomplish mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban gives Zilpah to Leah as her servant. In that culture, servants were given to strengthen a new household. I note the Lord sees every hidden person. Zilpah, though given in this bargain, will yet be used by God to bless the house of Jacob.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the morning, behold, it was Leah. Jacob cries out, 'Why then have you deceived me?' How piercing it is to reap what we sowed. Yet I am thankful that our sins are not dealt with in kind, but that Jesus bore our deception and our every transgression on the cross.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban appeals to the custom: the elder before the younger. This was the practice of that place, though it runs counter to the birthright Jacob had sought. The Lord often overturns man's customs to show that His purposes rest on grace, not merely on tradition.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fulfill the week of this one, and he will give Rachel also for seven more years of service. Leah is not cast off, but she is used as part of the bargain. My heart grieves for Leah, unloved by Jacob. But the Lord draws near to the unloved and will one day fully satisfy them in Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob does so and fulfills her week, then takes Rachel as wife. Love and labor are now divided between two sisters. What sorrow comes from seeking God's blessing by our own grasping. I pray the Lord would teach us to rest in His gifts, not to snatch them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Laban gives Bilhah to Rachel as her servant. Again, the Lord notes every servant. Bilhah, like Zilpah, will be named in the house of Israel. God uses the overlooked to build the family through whom He will bring our Savior.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah, and serves seven more years. The division of love brings division in the home. I have seen how favoritism wounds deeply. Thank God that in Jesus, our Savior, there is no favoritism - He loves all His own fully and equally.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh saw that Leah was hated, and He opened her womb, but Rachel was barren. The Lord sees the one whom man despises. He is not blind to affliction. How precious that He turns His attention to Leah in her sorrow and gives her the gift of children.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah bears Reuben and says, 'Because Yahweh has looked at my affliction... now my husband will love me.' Her hope is still in Jacob's love, yet the Lord is already drawing her to look to Him. I pray we would learn to look first to the One whose love for us is already full in Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She bears Simeon, saying Yahweh has heard that she is hated. Leah knows the Lord hears her. What comfort for the despised - the God who hears the cry of the lowly. He hears us still through the prayer of Jesus our great High Priest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Levi is born, and she hopes this time her husband will be joined to her. Three sons, yet the longing for Jacob's affection remains. Only the love of God in Christ can truly satisfy the deepest longing of our hearts. All other loves will fall short.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leah bears Judah and says, 'This time will I praise Yahweh.' At last her gaze turns from Jacob to the Lord. Readers today hear an echo of this grace: when our hopes in man fail, the Lord gently turns our eyes to praise Him. As of 2026-10, I am grateful He does the same for us in Jesus, our true Judah.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
